articles.title: The Silent Field Loss: Why a Green CI Pipeline is Lying to You
articles.excerpt: As an independent security researcher, I spend a lot of time auditing open-source cryptographic implementations and supply chain toolings. During a recent audit, I stumbled upon a terrifying realizati…
articles.body: As an independent security researcher, I spend a lot of time auditing open-source cryptographic implementations and supply chain toolings. During a recent audit, I stumbled upon a terrifying realization: Your CI is green, your schema validation passes, but the data might be silently disappearing. Here is the story of how we caught a silent field loss in a standard cryptographic data format, and why "structural validity" does not equal "semantic completeness." The Problem: Structural Validity vs. Semantic Loss When migrating to Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC), organizations rely on standardized formats like CycloneDX CBOM (Cryptographic Bill of Materials) to track algorithms. During our audit, we used a popular open-source Python library to parse and re-emit a CBOM document.

articles.title: TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'x') in JavaScript: 10 Causes and Fixes
articles.excerpt: "TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'x')" means you tried to read .x from a value that is undefined. The name in brackets is the property you asked for; the real problem is the th…
articles.body: "TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'x')" means you tried to read .x from a value that is undefined . The name in brackets is the property you asked for; the real problem is the thing before the dot. In user.address.city , if the error says (reading 'city') , then user.address is undefined. The fix is to find out why that value is missing (data not loaded yet, a function that forgot to return , a typo in a key, an array index past the end, or a lost this ) and either fix the cause or guard it with optional chaining: user.address?.city ?? "fallback" . This is probably the most common JavaScript error on the planet. It shows up in plain browser scripts, in Node.js, in React and Next.js apps, and in TypeScript projects that compiled without complaint.

articles.title: Paper Trading Crypto Futures: How to Make It Honest
articles.excerpt: Paper trading crypto futures means running a strategy or bot with simulated money on real market prices, so you can see how it behaves before risking capital. It is worth doing, but only if the simula…
articles.body: Paper trading crypto futures means running a strategy or bot with simulated money on real market prices, so you can see how it behaves before risking capital. It is worth doing, but only if the simulation includes fees, slippage, funding payments and liquidation rules. Without those, a paper result will usually look much better than the same strategy would look live. This guide shows how to set up an honest futures paper test, what to measure, and how to judge the result without fooling yourself. Why paper trading crypto futures is harder than spot Spot paper trading is simple: you buy, hold, and sell. Perpetual futures ("perps") add four costs and risks that many paper engines skip or simplify: Funding payments. Perps charge or pay funding at set intervals.

articles.body: If you pay for ChatGPT Plus, Pro, or Business — and you also use Codex — your subscription is about to work differently. Starting in December, OpenAI will fold ChatGPT and Codex into a single shared usage allowance, measured in tokens instead of message counts. Two buckets become one pool. The change came via a help-center document, not a big launch event. But for anyone who splits their day between chatting and coding, it matters. What is actually changing Today, chatbot conversations and coding sessions are metered independently. From December, Plus, Pro, and Business subscribers get one combined allowance across both products. Everything you do in ChatGPT's agent features and in Codex — through ChatGPT, your code editor, or the terminal — draws from the same pool.

articles.excerpt: Satellites are watching fireballs blaze through Earth's atmosphere, strengthening planetary defense knowhow and helping scientists learn more about space debris impacts.
articles.body: It came from outer space, exploding high above the South Atlantic off the coast of Argentina. That April 1 event — an incoming meteor , also termed a bolide — was observed by both U.S. space-based military and civil sensors. Hush-hush U.S. government satellite sensors detected the speedy fireball cutting through our atmosphere. The object's brightness peaked at an altitude of nearly 60 miles (90.5 kilometers) over the South Atlantic. That dazzling spectacle was also caught by the National Atmospheric and Oceanic Administration's GOES-E and Europe's Meteosat Third Generation (MTG) Imager-1 satellite. Those two independent spacecraft in geostationary orbit detected the bolide via onboard lightning imagers.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 1, 1962: The Soviet Union Launches Mars 1 spacecraft to Red Planet during the Space Race
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 1, 1962, the Soviet Union launched the Mars 1 spacecraft on a mission to fly by the Red Planet. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 1, 1962, the Soviet Union launched the Mars 1 spacecraft on a mission to fly by the Red Planet. While it did end up flying by Mars , the mission was not exactly a success. After it separated from the rocket, it deployed its solar panels and started cruising toward Mars. When mission controllers were checking out the telemetry it transmitted back to Earth, they found out that Mars 1 had sprung a leak in one of the gas valves that controls the spacecraft's orientation. And without a working orientation system, Mars 1 would have a hard time pointing its antennas in the right direction. It lost contact with Earth when it was about halfway to Mars . A model of Mars 1, a Mars flyby spacecraft launched to the Red Planet by the Soviet Union on Nov. 1, 1962.

articles.title: 5 bright planets to spot in November — when and where to see them
articles.excerpt: From a close encounter between Mars and Jupiter to dazzling Venus and elusive Mercury, November offers plenty of planetary highlights. Here's when and where to look.
articles.body: This is a great month for planet watching, either in the evenings or mornings. During convenient evening hours, the planet of choice is Saturn , visible well up in the southern sky during mid-to-late evening hours. Telescopically, the southern side of its famous ring system is currently tilted about 6½ degrees to our line of sight. Around the middle of the night, Mars and Jupiter come into view above the east-northeast horizon and just before the break of dawn are in excellent position, soaring high in the southern sky in the vicinity of the Sickle of Leo the Lion. Watch how Mars approaches Jupiter early in the month, passes it on Nov. 16, then spends the rest of the month sailing away to the east.

articles.title: Anthropic VS code extension on Cursor backdoored for nearly 12 hours
articles.excerpt: It's still unknown how attackers got access to Anthropic's verified Cursor account.
articles.body: An official extension for Anthropic’s Claude model was backdoored and threatened as many as 5,000 developers' machines, multiple sources reported Friday. Anthropic so far has yet to warn customers of the incident. The compromised package was a VS Code extension available in the marketplace of Cursor, a maker of AI-assisted developer tools, the company said Friday. The malicious version, 2.1.313, subsequently affected “at most 5,000 users,” presumably when they either downloaded it or their systems automatically fetched and installed it. Anthropic pushed version 2.1.314 several hours after the previous version became available on Cursor, according to independent researcher Kevin Beaumont.
